text: AI models hold skills no prompt can unlock. We enabled hidden skills inside Google's model through precise tuning of only a small number of its weights. TL;DR. AI models hold skills that no prompt can unlock. A NeurIPS 2025 study trained small numbers of randomly chosen weights in Llama and Qwen models of four sizes, across ten tasks: 10 to 100 trained weights closed up to half the gap between the original model and a fully fine-tuned one. We repeated the test on Google's smallest Gemma model, Gemma 3 270M. The best of 20 prompt wordings got it to sort five numbers correctly 1% of the time. After we trained 1,000 of its 100 million weights (0.001%), it sorted correctly 97% of the time. The same method switched on reversing word lists (84%) and clean JSON output (99% with 30 weights), and lifted long addition, while multiplication stayed near 30% even with 100,000 trained weights. In Quantifying Elicitation of Latent Capabilities in Language Models (NeurIPS 2025), Donoway and colleagues from Anthropic, UC Berkeley, Constellation, Thinking Machines and Scale AI fine-tuned only a few randomly selected weights and measured how much of a task the model could then do. Across Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5 models from 1B to 8B parameters and ten benchmark tasks, including science questions (ARC), yes/no reading questions (BoolQ), story writing (TinyStories) and chess puzzles: The authors' code is on GitHub . We wrote our own version for Gemma 3 270M, a model small enough to train on one 8 GB consumer GPU, and tested it on tasks a script can mark right or wrong. We asked the original Gemma 3 270M to sort five two-digit numbers in 20 different ways, 200 problems each: plain, polite, urgent, in capitals, in German, as a Python list, with a persona, step by step, "repeatedly take the smallest", and with one or three solved examples. The best wording, the Python list, scored 2 out of 200. Seventeen of the 20 scored zero. The usual reply returns the list unchanged: Sort these numbers in ascending order: 98, 37, 30, 59, 70. Answer with only the sorted numbers, separated by commas. 98, 37, 30, 59, 70 With a solved example in the prompt, the model sorted the example's numbers again and ignored the new list: Sort the numbers in ascending order. 42, 17, 88, 23, 61 -> 17, 23, 42, 61, 88 98, 37, 30, 59, 70 -> Here's the sorted list of numbers: 1. **17** 2. **23** 3. **42** 4. **61** 5. **88** Training a few weights unlocked it For each task we trained 10, 30, 100, 300, 1,000 or 100,000 randomly chosen weights, kept every other weight frozen, and scored the model on 500 problems it had not seen in training. Share of 500 test problems answered exactly right, by number of weights trained. JSON at 10 to 100 weights, and sorting, reversing and multiplying at 100 to 1,000 weights, are the average of three runs with different random picks. The other cells are one run. Gemma 3 270M adds three-digit numbers correctly 84% of the time and 12-digit numbers almost never. We compared 1,000 trained weights with full fine-tuning of the whole model, three runs each: The share of the gap that 1,000 weights closed fell from 85% at 3 digits to 29% at 12 digits. We tried the same method on four other behaviours. Each result came with a problem that limits what it shows. We took the 1,000-weight sorting run (98.8% correct) and tested its changes: The skill came from many small changes acting together. The 50 most damaging changes, trained alone, reached a quarter of the full result. Seven of the ten most damaging changes sat in attention output matrices, the part of each layer that writes attention's result back into the model. Restricting the random picks to those matrices helped: Sorting, average of three runs. Attention output was ahead or level in every run. We also tested a second way of choosing weights, which picks those whose input and output activations are most anti-correlated across the task's prompts. It needs only prompts, not answers. It added 2.2 to 4.6 points on 9- and 12-digit addition at 1,000 weights, and did worse than random picks on sorting with 10 to 100 weights (4.4% against 33% at 100 weights, one run each). The study trained randomly chosen weights inside low-rank adapters on Llama and Qwen. We trained randomly chosen weights of the model itself on Gemma.
